# Preface.

->§. 1.<-

Kind Reader, what I promised in the preface of my recently published *Supplements* <note>original: "Supplementis"; these were additional volumes or appendices the author had previously published to expand upon his primary work.</note>—namely, that I would present my system of the **Restoration of All Things** <term>Restoration of All Things: Also known as "Apocatastasis," this is the theological belief that all beings, including the damned and even the devil, will eventually be reconciled with God and saved.</term> in a very brief summary—I have hereby intended to properly fulfill.

§. 2. The reasons that moved me to write such a brief summary are various. The first main reason is this: because some complained that in my *System* <note>original: "Systema"; referring to the author’s comprehensive, structured theological framework.</note> I included far too many Latin words; a point which I have sought to improve very carefully in this brief summary. The other main reason is this: because our opponents complained that the system itself was far too lengthy for them to refute in order and point by point.

# Preface.

§. 3. The third main reason is this: because our opponents took the opportunity provided by such lengthiness to engage in all sorts of shadow-boxing. For they have completely abandoned the blade <note>The author uses dueling metaphors here to describe intellectual debate.</note>, and instead of attacking my arguments and the core matter, they have partially begun to judge my *System* <note>original: "Systema"</note> so broadly <note>original: "en general"</note> and to let their thoughts wander aimlessly into the open field as they pleased; indeed, they have attempted to win their spurs <note>original: "zu Rittern zu werden"; literally "to become knights," an idiom meaning to try and gain honor or status, in this case through petty attacks.</note> at my expense through mockery and slander.

§. 4. Now, the world certainly notices this, and sensible people laugh at it. However, I have also rightly considered how one might better constrain the opponents and bring them to a proper footing, so that they might either blush and lower their weapons, or in the future be forced to fight with greater sincerity.

§. 5. These, as stated, are the reasons that have moved me to the present brief summary. And indeed, in the first chapter, I have derived my conclusions not from mere reason, but rather from the **analogy of faith** <term>analogy of faith: A theological principle—originally "analogia fidei"—which suggests that individual Bible verses should be interpreted in the context of the whole of Christian doctrine rather than in isolation.</term> <note>original: "Aehnlichkeit des Glaubens"</note>.

§. 6. In the second chapter, I have shown that the **doctrine of restoration** <term>doctrine of restoration: Known as "Wiederbringungs-Lehre" or "Apocatastasis," the belief that all souls will eventually be reconciled to God.</term> may indeed be called an article of faith with every right.

do; namely, that I should have reasonably departed from the actual meaning of the words of Scripture in my explanations here and there. And in that case, they must be able to provide a sound and very important reason why I should have done so. For example, regarding **Romans 5:19**, I abide by the actual meaning of the word **render** <note>original: "Darstellen." In the context of 18th-century German theology, this refers to being "constituted" or "made" righteous, as found in the Greek text of Romans. The author is arguing for a literal fulfillment where all people are eventually made righteous.</note>, and simply believe that my **God** will one day **render** all and every person—not a single one excepted—righteous according to His wisdom, just as He promised there according to His truth. 

However, Mr. **Dr. Engelke** in **Rostock** <note>Bernhard Nicolaus Engelke (1704–1743) was a traditional Lutheran theologian who frequently engaged in polemics against those who taught the "Restoration of All Things" (universal salvation).</note> says: No, one must not accept the word **render** so simply here; rather, it means as much as: **God** will only *strive* to render all people righteous, even though the actual **rendering** will never happen to all people. I have clearly demonstrated this in this **Preface**, Section 50, etc., and anyone will be able to find the poor conclusions of this **Mr. Doctor** in the so-called **Honest Disclosure of the Theological Faculty at Rostock**, pages 59 and 60.

# Preface.

§. 17. For those who are rational, and especially those enlightened by **God**, will say: we do not need such a bogeyman <note>original: "popanz." A frightening figure or scarecrow used to instill fear; something used to scare children.</note> to terrify us. For to suffer eternal damnation <term>damnation: from "Verdammniß," referring to the state of being condemned to hell.</term> alongside the wretched devils <note>original: "unseelgen Teufeln." ...that the divine prophet <note>original Latin: "divinum vatem," referring here to the author of the biblical text, likely Isaiah or the Evangelist Mark</note> intended this: that those torments, viewed in themselves, were never to be finished, yet God would at some time establish an end and a measure for them. What can be clearer and more distinct than these words: **Their worm shall not die / and their fire shall not be extinguished?** Thus, Gerhard does not venture to deny that it may be quite correctly concluded from these words that that which causes the torment and pain in damned humans remains constant (namely, because it has no **principle of destruction** <note>original Latin: "principium destructionis," a philosophical term for an internal force or element that causes a thing to break down or end</note> within itself): however, Gerhard denies that it can be proven from these same cited prophetic words that God (as the **principle of destruction**, which the worm and the fire have above them) will not one day [bring an end to] the punishment and pain...

§. 113. Reverend Sir, my proposition, which is contained within the Prophetic saying <note>Refers to Isaiah 66:24: "their worm shall not die."</note>, is this: The **Hellish worm** has no **principle of destruction** <term>Latin: *principium destructionis*; an internal mechanism or natural necessity that causes a thing to eventually break down and die</term> within itself, such that it must finally perish from old age and weakness, as one observes in a worm of this world. The **bottom line** <note>original: *Das Ende vom Liede*; literally "the end of the song," an idiom for the final result or conclusion</note> is therefore this: that Mr. Buddeus must give me a reason why I should abandon the clear context in the **Pauline passage** <note>referring to the writings of the Apostle Paul, specifically Romans 5:19</note> and, through the latter "many," understand only the few believers, while through the first "many," understanding all people. ## Preface.

...[al]ways <note>The text begins with a fragment, likely "immer" (always) or "nimmer" (never).</note> remain with the Divine unfathomable love, alongside their otherwise so highly-praised **principles** <note>original Latin: *principiis*</note> and dogmas, just as well as the hare stays by the drum <note>A German idiom "wie der Hase bei der Trommel," referring to someone who is terrified, confused, or completely out of place in a situation they cannot escape or understand.</note>. §. 196. The sin of Adam and his unblessed effort have already been addressed: therefore, in the opening clause <note>original: *Vorsatz*; in logic and rhetoric, this refers to the first part of a sentence or the "protasis" of the verse</note> of the 19th verse, it cannot again be a matter of that same imputation <note>the legal crediting of Adam's sin to his descendants</note> and that same effort. Rather, the discussion must now instead be about the actual application <note>the point at which the state of sin actually takes root within a person</note>.

The second reason he will give is this: because Adam’s sin could not simply remain a matter of mere imputation and mere effort; instead, the sinful corruption <note>original: *Verderbniß*</note> had to be actually applied to all descendants as well.

And finally, your opponent's third reason will be this: because in the 19th verse, the Apostle speaks of "actually presenting" <note>the German *darstellen* translates the Greek *kathistēmi*, meaning to be constituted or rendered</note>, a word—"presenting"—which he had not used in the preceding 18th verse. Consequently, if all people were to be presented as actual sinners, then sin must also be actually applied to each and every person; otherwise, one would have to conceive of an actual "presenting" without "application," which would be so foolish that nothing could be more absurd.

See there, dear soul, in such a way your opponent will now reach the entirely infallible conclusion themselves: that in the opening clause of the 19th verse, it is necessarily a matter of the actual application of sinful corruption.

Adam’s sin and his miserable effort have been dealt with: then in the opening clause of the 19th verse, the discussion cannot again be about that same imputation <term>Imputation: the legal reckoning of guilt or righteousness to a person's account</term> and that same effort; rather, the discussion must now instead be about the actual application <term>Application: the point at which a theological truth becomes an internal, lived reality within a person</term>. The reason, he will say, is,

secondly, this: because it could not remain with Adam’s sin merely as a matter of the mere imputation and the mere effort; instead, the sinful corruption <note>original: *sündliche Verderbniß*; the inherent tainted nature of humanity following the Fall</note> also had to be actually applied to all descendants. And finally, your opponent’s third reason will be this: Because the Apostle, in the 19th verse, speaks of an actual presentation <note>original: *darstellen*; this refers to the Greek word *kathistemi* used in Romans 5:19, often translated as "made" or "constituted" (e.g., "many were made sinners")</note>, which word—"present"—he had not used in the preceding 18th verse.

Consequently, where all people were to be presented as actual sinners, then sin must also be actually applied to each and every person; otherwise, one would have to conceive of an actual presentation without application, which would be so foolish that nothing could be more foolish. Behold, dear soul, in such a way your opponent himself will now make the entirely infallible conclusion that in the opening clause of the 19th verse, the discussion is necessarily about the actual application of sinful corruption.

# of the Restoration.

Poisoning and discord—they are reconciled through **Christ** once again; I say, they are reconciled, not only with one another and with the rest of the creatures, but also to Christ as their supreme Head. This is because they are once more placed under his feet and are re-headed <term>re-headed</term> <note>original: *wieder behauptet*; a theological term for "recapitulation," or bringing all things back under the authority of Christ as the "head" of creation.</note>, as the Psalmist has taught us from the previously cited **8th Psalm**, as has Paul. Indeed, the wretched creature longs for this *applicative* reconciliation and re-heading as if with an **outstretched neck** <note>The German *ausgerecktem Halse* is a literal translation of the Greek *apokaradokia* in Romans 8:19, depicting someone leaning forward with intense, strained expectation.</note> and is in constant anguish, *Romans 8:19 and 22.* For the preceding 21st verse indicates that there will truly be an *applicative* reconciliation: because even the irrational creature itself shall be set free from the service of **decay** <note>original: *vergänglichen Wesens*; often translated in Bibles as the "bondage of corruption."</note> into the glorious freedom of the children of **God**.

### 1 Timothy 4:10

> **GOD is a Savior of all men, especially of those who believe.**

In this one single verse, there is a single predicate <term>predicate; in logic and grammar, the part of a sentence that states something about the subject</term>, namely being a **Savior**, which is not at all ambiguous. Furthermore, there are found in this same verse two opposites <note>original: *Opposita*</note> (or things set against one another), namely the entire godless world, or all men, and then the believers. Now, just as **God** is a **Savior** of the believers—not only acquisitively <term>acquisitive; referring to the merit or "acquisition" of salvation through Christ's work</term> (as if He had merely earned such for the believers—No!) but also applicatively <term>applicative; referring to the actual application or practical realization of that salvation to the person</term>—so also, by virtue of this contrast, must this same **God** be a **Savior** of the entire godless world, not only acquisitively, but also applicatively. Consequently, the entire godless world must also finally be truly saved <note>original: *seelig*; can mean blessed, happy, or eternally saved</note>, though in its own order, even if it should take as long as it will.

# On the Verses
## which are usually cited as proof of unending damnation.

§. 4. Listen, dear soul, if we wish to proceed uprightly and as is fitting in the explanation of this verse, we must arrange everything precisely according to our opponents’ own <term>exegetical principles</term> <note>These are the formal rules of interpretation used by theologians to determine the meaning of biblical texts.</note>; for otherwise, we would not reach an understanding with them.

§. 5. Our opponents, you see, have a splendid rule, which reads as follows:
> In the explanation of Scripture, one must by no means deviate from the literal meaning of the words, unless the nature of the matter, the <term>analogy of Scripture</term> <note>original: *Analogie der Schrifft*; the theological principle that any individual passage must be interpreted in harmony with the rest of the Bible’s teachings.</note>, and the clear circumstances of the text should inescapably require it.

§. 6. Well then, we wish to observe this "golden rule" of our adversaries most precisely. It is asked, therefore: what does the phrase *to die* and *not to die* mean in its literal and exact sense within the prophetic verse? Answer: *To die*, in its formal, literal meaning, signifies as much as: **to lose the powers of life and movement.** Such a meaning is gladly and willingly accepted by our opponents themselves, as can be seen in the work of <term>David Hollaz</term> <note>David Hollaz (1648–1713) was a prominent Lutheran systematic theologian whose "Examen Theologicum Acroamaticum" was a standard textbook of the era.</note> in his *Examen Theologicum*, Part III, Section II, Chapter 9, Question 3, page 374.

# of an Infinite Damnation.

§. 7. Now a living thing can lose its **life forces** <note>original: *Lebens-Kräffte*</note> in a twofold manner: namely, either through the **principle of destruction** <note>original: *Principium destructionis*</note> that is within the thing itself <margin>In German, one might render the "principle of destruction" thus: A power promoting downfall.</margin>; or also through such a principle of destruction which is outside and above the thing.

§. 8. For example: man, after the **Fall** <note>The biblical account of Adam and Eve's first sin, which theologians of this era believed introduced physical death into the world.</note>, can lose his life forces and die in both ways. First, he can lose his life forces through the principle of destruction that is within him. For when the **radical moisture and radical heat** <term>radical moisture and heat</term> <note>original: *humor and calor radicalis*. In the medical understanding of the time (derived from Galen), these were the innate fluids and warmth that fueled the body; their exhaustion led to "natural death" from old age.</note> within him gradually decrease through internal **disharmony**, then man must indeed finally perish and die of old age. Secondly, man can also lose his life forces through a principle of destruction that is outside and above him; and that, in turn, in a twofold way: either through a **created principle of destruction**, if he, for example, drowns in water or burns in fire, etc.; or he loses his life forces through the **Divine principle of destruction**, which can cut the **thread of life** <note>original: *Lebens-Faden*; a common metaphor for the span of a person's life, originally referring to the Fates of mythology.</note> at his pleasure.

§. 9.

# Refutation of the Proof-Passages
<meta>catchword: Passage</meta>

... <term>principle of destruction</term> <note>original Latin: *Principium destructionis*; the internal or external cause that leads to the end of a thing's existence</note>, which the worm has above itself, has so willed and desired it, as to not <term>destroy</term> <note>original: *destruiren*</note> the Hellish Worm.

§. 17. Our opponents now affirm this, and wish to forcefully assert that God has firmly resolved not to destroy or annihilate the Hellish Worm throughout all infinite eternity.

§. 18. But from where do our opponents prove this? "Yes," they say, "we prove it from the disputed prophetic passage:
> their worm will not die." <note>A reference to Mark 9:44 or Isaiah 66:24, traditionally used to argue for never-ending punishment in hell.</note>

§. 19. Answer: that is a very foolish way to prove something by <term>begging the question</term> <note>original Latin: *per petitionem principii*; a logical fallacy where the speaker assumes the truth of the very thing they are trying to prove.</note>. For the Divine Will is not contained within that passage—namely, that the Divine principle of destruction does not want to destroy or annihilate the worm. Rather, it is only stated <term>in general</term> <note>original French: *en general*</note> and broadly that the worm will not die, nor lose its gnawing powers.

Now, however, the worm can lose its tormenting power in a twofold manner, as we have heard: either through a principle of destruction within itself, or through a principle of destruction above it. # Refutation of the Proof-Texts

can one prove an infinity from the figure of speech <note>original: "Redens-Art"</note> itself—namely, from the "not dying" and "not being extinguished"? Answer: by no means! For where the mentioned figure of speech is used **Firstly** regarding an object of which it has already been proven elsewhere that it has an end, then it certainly does not mean the same as "infinite." For example: when it is said of the hero Gideon <note>Referring to the biblical judge; the author likely references a specific interpretation where temporal things are described with "eternal" phrasing</note>, and of the fire on the altar <note>See Leviticus 6:13; though called a "continual" fire, the physical altar and its fire eventually ceased to exist</note>, that they do not die and are not extinguished: then our adversaries <note>theological opponents who argue for eternal hellfire</note> themselves teach that the expression "not dying" and "not being extinguished" does not, in itself, signify an infinity in those cases.

Secondly, however, if the same figure of speech is used for an object of which it has already been established elsewhere that it has no end: then indeed "not dying" and "not being extinguished" means as much as: to live and burn infinitely; but truly not by virtue of the figure of speech itself, but by virtue of the object for which the figure of speech is used. For example: when it is said of God and of the holy angels that they do not die; or when one must say of the figurative <note>original: "verblühmten," meaning flowery or metaphorical</note> fire of God's love that it never goes out: then such figures of speech do indeed indicate an infinity, but only by virtue of the object to which they are attached.

My proposition is this: *Eternal* in the whole of Holy Scripture never signifies as much as "infinite"; understood in and of itself, formally <note>original: "formaliter"</note>, by its own nature <note>original: "sua natura"</note>, and through itself <note>original: "& per se"</note>.

**§. 89.** For formally <note>original: "formaliter"</note> "eternal" signifies a length of duration <note>original: "diuturnitatem"</note> that is either infinite <note>original: "infinita"</note>, or which only lasts as long as the object of which it speaks can endure it, yet in such a way that its end is unknown to us, or indefinite <note>original: "indefinita"</note>.

## §. 14.
But one might say: such a wealthy clergyman will surely prepare himself properly on his deathbed—that is, he will confess his sins and thereafter receive **Holy Communion** <term>Abendmahl; also known as the Lord's Supper or the Eucharist</term>. # Doctrine of Restitution

One sees this clearly, among other examples, from Johann Christoph Coler’s *History of Gottfried Arnold*. <note>Gottfried Arnold (1666–1714) was a controversial radical Pietist whose writings on church history often defended "heretics," making him a target for the Lutheran establishment.</note> Specifically, the highly renowned Mr. Gottlieb Wernsdorf <note>A leading orthodox Lutheran theologian known for his defense of traditional doctrine.</note> wrote a preface for the aforementioned book, in which he disputes, among other things: whether one could believe that Arnold was saved? He refers specifically to the rule of the Church Father Augustine: **The sin is not forgiven where the stolen property is not restored.** <note>original: "Non remittitur peccatum, nisi restituatur ablatum." # The Doctrine of Restoration does not make one secure.

§. 61. See, my dear friend, try it for once, to see if you can pray thus with an honest heart and without hypocrisy! Be so good as to give me your answer on that! Truly, I say to you, you will find that **flesh and blood** <term>Fleisch und Blut: A biblical term for human nature in its fallen, weak, and selfish state, as opposed to the spirit.</term> will not be willing to engage in this prayer, and it requires a great struggle to sacrifice oneself so completely to the will of God in true sincerity and without the slightest exception. I ask you, believe me!

§. 62. I will grant, however, that you came so far, and your sighing to God was righteous: Oh, then you must certainly not think that this is already true Christianity! No, my dear friend, for now the battle only truly begins! For since God has now given you the *will*, you must now day and night, unceasingly, persist with him, that he might also grant you the *accomplishment*: seeing as he has promised both in his Word <note>A reference to Philippians 2:13: "For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure."</note>.

And under these circumstances, flesh and blood only then notice that they are meant to die: against this, however, it resists with hand and mouth, and you will find that now the innermost depths of your evil heart will be truly uncovered; yes, you will get to see so many tricks and corners of your flesh and blood that you will be horrified by it. But this cannot be helped; instead, you must go through it. Your God, who has once seized you, and to whom you have honestly sacrificed yourself, he will not leave you: his own honor depends on it, he cannot deny himself! Just take the risk with the dear God: Persevere honestly with him for the first seven years. And if it were then perhaps only the weak **Leah** <note>In Genesis 29, Jacob works seven years for Rachel but is given her sister Leah first; the author uses this to represent the initial, perhaps less beautiful or more difficult stages of spiritual labor.</note>, then endure the other seven years with joy as well, and so on and so forth, so you will finally win your **little wreath** <note>original: "Cräntzlein"; a symbol of spiritual victory or the "crown of life."</note>. May God help me and all well-meaning souls toward this, for the sake of Jesus Christ’s wounds, AMEN!

Go now and say: that the **Restoration Doctrine** <term>Wiederbringungs-Lehre: Also known as Universal Restoration or Apokatastasis; the belief that all fallen beings will eventually be reconciled to God.</term> leads to complacency!

<meta>This page continues the argument from the title page, where the author, Johann Konrad Dippel, begins his specific theological defense regarding the fate of Judas Iscariot. <image-desc>A decorative rectangular woodcut headpiece featuring a central stylized flower resembling a sunflower, surrounded by ornate, symmetrical acanthus leaf scrolls and floral motifs in a baroque style.</image-desc>

The *utterance* <note>original: "Expression"</note> of the Savior concerning Judas, the traitor: *It would be better for him if he had not been born*, cannot be properly understood either by the *Orthodox* <note>The established church authorities of the 18th century who upheld the doctrine of eternal damnation.</note> or by those who believe in the *Restoration of All Things* <term>Restoration of All Things: Also known as "Apokatastasis," the belief that all souls will eventually be reconciled with God.</term>. This is because neither of them *presumes* that the Savior, in his speeches, very often made use of the *idioms* <note>original: "Formulen"</note> of the Jewish *Synagogue*, insofar as their meaning was not *directly* <note>original: "directè"</note> opposed to his *Gospel*. The Englishman *Allix* <note>Pierre Allix (1641–1717), a prominent theologian who argued that many Christian concepts were rooted in early Jewish traditions.</note> has sufficiently demonstrated this in his *Treatise on the Trinity* <note>original: "Tractat de Trinitate"</note>, and many traces of such *accommodation* <term>Theological Accommodation: The idea that Jesus adapted his language to the existing cultural and religious concepts of his audience so they could understand him.</term> are found in the history of the Evangelists, especially in the *subject matter* pertaining to this case, which alone can *provide* the correct explanation for this pronouncement of the Savior.

...[from] the followers of **Hermes** in Egypt, and borrowed from his students among the Greeks—the **Pythagoreans** and **Platonists**—or whether this philosophy first came from the **Patriarchs of the Jews** to the Egyptians and the other **Heathens**, cannot well be demonstrated with certainty. -> ) 0 ( <-

[Whether the error of the Manichaeans is not more tolerable than the views of] today's Orthodox, or also the Boehmists <note>Followers of the German mystic Jakob Böhme (1575–1624), who taught complex ideas about the struggle between light and dark within the divine nature</note>, who recognize that light and darkness, good and evil, first became revealed and set against one another in time; but nevertheless maintain that darkness, as well as light, shall bring forth its births into all eternities of eternities, and remain opposed to the light?
